claims.text: A data-driven, defect-inclusive approach will improve conductivity-prediction accuracy for bulk HfNbTaTiZr relative to standard analytical models.
The proposed accuracy improvement will apply in the 0–200 K regime.
The proposed accuracy improvement will apply in the 300–1200 K regime.
Conductivity measurements are available for a HfNbTaTiZr specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen in the 300–1200 K regime.
The relevant bulk HfNbTaTiZr state may be as-cast or sintered and near equilibrium.
Oxygen-related defects and microstructural imperfections modify electron scattering.
Oxygen-related defects and microstructural imperfections modify phonon contributions to conductivity.
Training on ideal and defect-bearing microstructures enables a model to capture the effects of oxygen impurities and structural disorder on carrier scattering.
Including defect-bearing microstructures makes the model more representative of realistic samples than perfect-lattice analytical predictions.
The proposed model will have lower conductivity-prediction error than analytical models that ignore defects.
At approximately 500 K, the proposed model's predicted conductivity will be within ±10% of the measured value.
At approximately 500 K, existing analytical models will deviate from measurement by more than the proposed model.
Standard perfect-crystal analytical predictions show significant deviations from experiment when oxygen contamination is present.
Standard analytical predictions show significant deviations from experiment at low- and high-temperature extremes.
The expected advantage is limited to oxygen levels around 1 wt.% and processing conditions similar to those represented in the training data.
Predictions may be less reliable for substantially different oxygen concentrations or impurity types absent from the training data.
The reduction in prediction error may be 10–30%, but its exact magnitude is uncertain.
The model's ability to capture low-temperature phonon scattering and quantum effects remains unvalidated.
Held-out conductivity measurements at 150 K and 500 K can benchmark the proposed model against standard analytical predictions.
Failure to reduce prediction error in either temperature regime, including deviation exceeding 10%, would falsify the hypothesis.
